deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is folio 13 of Riemann's Paris prize essay on heat conduction (the 1861 'Commentatio mathematica', printed posthumously in the Werke, 1876). The problem is to decide when a quadratic form Σ b_{ij} ds_i ds_j can be transformed into a form with constant coefficients (equivalently Σ dx_i^2). The previous page derived the curvature quantities (ii',i''i''') ~ R_{ijkl}. It formed the expression II = Σ R_{ijkl} (ds∧δs)^{ij} (ds∧δs)^{kl}, summed over pairs i<j and k<l, and the quotient
  III: K(ds,δs) = (1/2) Σ R_{ijkl} p^{ij} p^{kl} / [ g(ds,ds) g(δs,δs) − g(ds,δs)^2 ],
with p^{ij} = ds_i δs_j − ds_j δs_i, up to the sign normalisation noted by Riemann ('mit −1 multiplicirt').

Step 1 (top of page). III is unchanged under a change of independent variables. Since II and the Gram determinant are tensorial, this was already stated on p.12. It is also unchanged if (ds, δs) is replaced by (a ds + b δs, c ds + d δs) with ad − bc ≠ 0. [Filled in by me:] each bivector component p^{ij} is multiplied by (ad − bc), so the numerator gets the factor (ad − bc)^2. The Gram determinant gets the same factor. So K depends only on the 2-plane spanned by ds and δs at the point; this is the modern sectional curvature K(σ).

Step 2. The maximum and minimum values of K over all planes at a point do not depend on the coordinate form chosen or on the particular ds, δs. They are scalar invariants of the metric. Riemann says that from them one can recognise whether two such forms can be transformed into each other.

Step 3 (geometric interpretation, 'conceptibus inusitatis'). √(Σ b_{ij} ds_i ds_j) is the line element of an n-dimensional space beyond intuition. Draw all shortest lines (geodesics) from the point s whose initial directions are α ds + β δs. They sweep out a surface, which can be developed/realised in ordinary space. Expression III is then the (Gaussian) curvature of this surface at s. This is exactly the definition of sectional curvature in his 1854 Habilitationsvortrag, here tied to the analytic formula.

Step 4 (n = 3). II is a quadratic form in the three bivector components (ds_2δs_3 − ds_3δs_2, ds_3δs_1 − ds_1δs_3, ds_1δs_2 − ds_2δs_1). A symmetric 3×3 form has 6 coefficients. So there are six equations R_{ijkl} = 0 that the b must satisfy for reducibility to constant coefficients. In 3D these are equivalent to Ric = 0, since n^2(n^2−1)/12 = 6.
- Sufficiency: Riemann asserts that, with the notions just explained, these six conditions are demonstrably sufficient.
- Independence: only three are 'entirely independent'. In modern terms this reflects the three differential (contracted Bianchi) identities ∇^i G_{ij} = 0 linking the six components.

Step 5. To answer the Academy's question, one substitutes the forms of b found earlier by the 'method set out above' into these six equations. This would give all cases in which the temperature u in homogeneous bodies can be a function of time and only two variables. Riemann says lack of time prevented carrying out the calculations, and he will only list the solutions (done on the next page).
errors: Overstatement: the max and min of the sectional curvature at a point are necessary invariants but do not by themselves decide whether two forms are equivalent in general. Full equivalence needs the whole curvature tensor and its covariant derivatives (Christoffel 1869). For the flat case at issue (K ≡ 0) the criterion is fine.

Sufficiency of the six conditions is only asserted ('est demonstratu'), not proved on this page. It is true (Riemann–Lipschitz–Christoffel), and Riemann's own argument presumably used normal/geodesic coordinates.
'Only three entirely independent' is imprecise. The six equations are algebraically independent; the dependence is differential (Bianchi identities), not algebraic.
Sign/normalisation of III relative to modern K depends on the convention flagged by the marginal note on p.12 (multiplication by −1). No substantive error.

results.what: Quotient III is invariant under coordinate change and under change of basis of the 2-plane spanned by ds, δs
Geometric meaning: curvature of the surface swept out by geodesics tangent to the plane
results.modern_name: Riemann's definition of sectional curvature via geodesic surfaces

results.what: In n = 3 the flatness conditions are six equations R_{ijkl} = 0, sufficient for reduction to constant coefficients
results.modern_name: Flatness criterion (vanishing Riemann tensor ⇔ locally Euclidean); in 3D Ric = 0
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1861; proofs by Christoffel and Lipschitz 1869–70

results.what: Only three of the six conditions are independent
results.modern_name: Consequence of the contracted Bianchi identities

results.what: Max/min of the curvature as invariants to test equivalence of quadratic differential forms
results.modern_name: Curvature invariants / equivalence problem for metrics

deep.surprise_reason: This page is part of Riemann's Paris prize essay. It is published in his Werke (1876) and extensively studied (e.g. Weber's notes, Farwell & Knee 1990). The sectional-curvature formula and the 'three independent' remark, often read as anticipating the Bianchi identities, are already known as his.

checkable.asserts: The denominator of III scales by (ad−bc)^2 under a change of basis of the plane (result 0).
Bivector components scale by (ad−bc), so the numerator II scales by (ad−bc)^2 and III is invariant (result 0).
The number of independent curvature components in 3 dimensions is 6, matching Riemann's six equations.
